**Surat al-Hujurat**
Eighteen verses, Medinan (Madaniyyah)

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

﴿O you who have believed, do not put [yourselves] before Allah and His Messenger, and fear Allah. Indeed, Allah is Hearing and Knowing.﴾

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

﴿O you who have believed, do not put [yourselves] before Allah and His Messenger, and fear Allah. Indeed, Allah is Hearing and Knowing.﴾.

Concerning the explanation of the excellence of this arrangement, there are several aspects:

The first: In the preceding surah, when some of them inclined toward refusal regarding what the Prophet ﷺ had accepted of the peace treaty, and the omission of the phrase of the basmala and of the title "Messenger of Allah," and he (ﷺ) obliged them to the word of piety, it was as if the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had said to them in general terms: Do not put [yourselves] before Allah and His Messenger, and do not go beyond what Allah the Exalted and His Messenger command.

The second: When Allah the Exalted described the station of the Prophet, peace be upon him, and the loftiness of his rank by making him His Messenger who makes His religion manifest, and mentioned that he is compassionate to the believers by His saying: ﴿compassionate﴾ [al-Tawbah: 128], He said: Do not leave any part of his reverence, neither in deed nor in word, and do not be deceived by his kindness, and consider the elevation of his rank.

The third: Allah the Exalted described the believers as being ﴿severe against the disbelievers, merciful among themselves, [seen] bowing and prostrating﴾ [al-Fath: 29], looking to the side of Allah the Exalted, and He mentioned that they have from honor with Allah what has brought them good praise in the earlier Books, by His saying: ﴿That is their likeness in the Torah, and their likeness in the Gospel﴾ [al-Fath: 29]. For a great king does not mention anyone in his absence unless that person is honored in his presence. And He promised them a great reward. So He said in this surah: Do not do what necessitates the lowering of your rank and the nullifying of your good deeds, and ﴿do not put [yourselves] before﴾.

It was said: Concerning the occasion of the revelation of the verse there are several reports. It was said: It was revealed concerning fasting on the day of doubt (yawm al-shakk). It was said: It was revealed concerning sacrificing before the Eid prayer. It was said: It was revealed concerning three men who killed two men from Sulaym, whom they thought were from Banu Amir. It was said: It was revealed concerning a group who asked excessively, and delegations had come to the Prophet ﷺ. The most correct view is that it is a general guidance that encompasses all of these, and an absolute prohibition that includes every assertion, every advancing, every acting on one's own authority in a matter, and every undertaking of an action that is not necessary without consultation.

In the interpretation there are several issues:

The first issue: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿do not put [yourselves] before﴾ (lā tuqaddimū) may carry two meanings:

One of them: That it is from "taqdīm" (putting forward), which is transitive. On this basis there are two views:

The first: The omission of its object altogether, as in His saying: ﴿He gives life and causes death﴾ [al-Baqarah: 258], and the saying of a speaker: "So-and-so gives and withholds," where he does not mean by them the giving of a specific thing or the withholding of a specific thing, but rather means that he has the capacity for withholding and giving. Likewise here, as if He, Exalted is He, were saying: It should not proceed from you any putting forward at all.

The second: That the object is the act or the command, as if He were saying: ﴿do not put forward﴾ meaning an act ﴿before Allah and His Messenger﴾, or: do not put forward a command. The second meaning: That what is intended is "do not put forward" in the sense of "do not advance" (lā tataqaddamū). On this basis it is a metaphor, and the intended meaning is not the act of putting forward itself, but rather: do not make for yourselves an advancement in the presence of the Prophet ﷺ. It is said: "So-and-so advanced among the people" when his affair became elevated and his status exalted. The reason for this is that whoever is elevated is advanced in entering great matters and in being mentioned when the noble are mentioned. On this basis we say: whether we make it transitive or intransitive, the putting forward does not extend to it in our saying "I put forward Zayd." So its implied meaning is: do not put yourselves forward in the presence of the Prophet ﷺ, that is, do not make for yourselves an advancement and an opinion in his presence. We do not say that what is meant is "do not put forward a command or an act." In that case the two readings agree in meaning: the reading of the one who reads with a fatḥah on the tā' and dāl, and the reading of the one who reads with a ḍammah on the tā' and a kasrah on the dāl.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿before Allah and His Messenger﴾ means: in their presence. For what is in the presence of a person is "before his hands" (bayna yadayh), and he sees it, and it is before his eyes. And in His saying ﴿before Allah and His Messenger﴾ there are benefits:

The first: That the saying of a speaker, "So-and-so is before So-and-so," is an indication that each of the two is present in the presence of the other, although one of them has a lofty rank and the other has the degree of servants and attendants. For whoever sits beside a person requires him to turn his eyeball toward him and to move his head toward him when speaking and when giving commands, whereas whoever sits before him does not require that of him. Also, the two hands indicate power. One says: "He is before So-and-so," meaning he turns him however he wishes in his affairs, just as a person does with what is placed before his hands. And this indicates the obligation to avoid putting oneself forward and advancing oneself, for one who is like a piece of goods that a person turns over in his hands—how could he have any precedence before him?

The second: Mentioning Allah is an indication of the obligation to revere the Messenger, peace be upon him, and to submit to his commands. This is because reverence for the Messenger ﷺ may be neglected due to the distance of the one who sent him and his not being aware of what is done to His Messenger. So He said: ﴿before Allah﴾, meaning: you are in the presence of Allah the Exalted, and He is watching you. In such a situation it is obligatory to revere His Messenger.

The third: That this expression, as established, is the prohibition that came earlier, and it establishes the meaning of the command that comes later, which is His saying: "and fear" (wa-ttaqū). For whoever is before another like goods placed before him, who does with him whatever he wishes, is deserving of being wary of him. His saying, Exalted is He: "and fear Allah" (wa-ttaqū Allāh) may be a conjunction that requires a difference, like the difference in the saying of a speaker: "Do not sleep and occupy yourself." That is, the benefit of that prohibition is what is in this command, and what is required by it is not abandoning sleep in any way, but rather the occupation. So likewise: do not put yourselves forward, and do not advance in a manner of piety. It is also possible that between the two there is a more complete difference, which is the one in the saying of a speaker: "Revere Zayd and serve him," that is, bring the most complete reverence. Likewise here, its meaning: do not advance in his presence. And if you abandon advancing, do not rely upon that and so not benefit from it; rather, even though you stand by it and revere him, fear Allah and be in awe of Him, for otherwise you would not have brought the obligation of reverence.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Hearing and Knowing﴾ confirms what preceded, because they said "We have believed," since the address is understood from His saying: "O you who have believed." So He hears their saying and knows their action and what is in their hearts of piety and treachery. Therefore it is not fitting that your speech, your action, and the inner state of your hearts should differ. Rather, what He hears of your saying, "We have believed, we have heard, and we have obeyed," and what He knows of your outward action, which is not putting yourselves forward, and what is in your hearts of inner states, which is piety, should all be complete.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿O you who believe, do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet, and do not speak loudly to him as you speak loudly to one another, lest your deeds become worthless while you do not perceive.﴾

﴿Do not put [yourselves] forward﴾ is a prohibition against an act that indicates their placing themselves, in relation to Allah and His Messenger, in a position of weight, rank and standing in one of their commands and prohibitions. His saying ﴿do not raise﴾ is a prohibition against a speech that indicates that same matter, because whoever raises his voice in the presence of another gives himself consideration and greatness. In this are several issues:

The first issue: What is the benefit of repeating the call, and what is this pattern of two statements, in the saying of the One who says: ﴿O you who believe, do not put [yourselves] forward before Allah﴾ and ﴿do not raise your voices﴾? We say: there are five benefits in repeating the call. Among them is that it shows increased compassion toward the one seeking guidance, as in Luqman's saying to his son: ﴿O my son, do not associate anything with Allah﴾ [Luqman: 13], ﴿O my son, indeed it [the deed], if it should be the weight of a mustard seed﴾ [Luqman: 16], ﴿O my son, establish prayer﴾ [Luqman: 17]. This is because the call serves to alert the one being addressed so that he will attend to the speech and give it his attention, so repeating it serves that purpose. Among them is that no one should suppose that the one addressed second is other than the one addressed first. It is permissible for a speaker to say: "O Zayd, do such-and-such, and say such-and-such, O 'Amr." But when he repeats it once more and says: "O Zayd, say such-and-such," it is known from the beginning of the speech that he is also the one addressed second. Among them is that it is made known that each of the two statements is intended, and that the second is not an emphasis of the first. As you say: "O Zayd, do not utter [anything], and do not speak except with the truth," it would not be good to say: "O Zayd, do not utter; O Zayd, do not speak," as it would be good when the two demands differ. The saying of the Exalted, ﴿do not raise your voices﴾, admits of several aspects:

One of them: that its intended meaning is its literal sense, because raising the voice is a sign of little modesty and of abandoning reverence. This relates to a legal-physical matter, namely that the voice comes out through the vocal organs, and whoever's heart fears is startled, and his driving motion weakens, so the voice does not come out of him with force. Whoever does not fear, his heart remains steady and strong, so raising the voice is evidence of the absence of fear.

The second aspect: that the intended meaning is prohibition of excessive speech, because whoever speaks much speaks while others are silent, so in the time of others' silence his voice is raised, even if he is afraid when you look at the state of others. It is not fitting that anyone should have much speech in the presence of the Prophet ﷺ in comparison with the speech of the Prophet ﷺ, because the Prophet, upon him be prayer and peace, is a conveyor [of the message]. So one who speaks in his presence to inform [him] is not permitted, and if he asks the Prophet, upon him be peace, about what he is obligated to explain, [the Prophet] does not remain silent about what is asked even if it is not asked. Perhaps in the question there is an attempt to put [him] to a response that is not easy for the mukallaf (legally accountable person) to give, so he remains in the peril of punishment.

The third aspect: that the intended meaning is raising speech through exalting it, i.e., do not make your speech elevated above the speech of the Prophet ﷺ in address, as one says to another: "I have told you many times to do such-and-such" when his companion says to him: "Command me with a command like it." So one of the two statements is higher and loftier than the other. The first is more correct, and all of them fall under the ruling of what is intended, because the prohibition against raising the voice occurs only for the sake of reverence and showing modesty. Whoever's reverence reaches the point where voices are lowered before him, out of awe of him and the loftiness of his rank, will not have much speech before him, nor will the speaker return to argue with him in address.

The saying of the Exalted, ﴿and do not speak loudly to him as you speak loudly to one another﴾, contains benefits:

The first: that by the former [clause] the prohibition has been established against a person making his speech or voice higher than the speech and voice of the Prophet ﷺ. One might say: what has the prohibition prevented from equality? So He said: ﴿and do not speak loudly to him as you speak loudly to your peers and equals,﴾ but rather make his word the highest.

The second: that this indicates that a believer should not speak in the presence of the Prophet, upon him be peace, as a slave speaks in the presence of his master, because the slave falls under the saying ﴿as you speak loudly to one another﴾, since it is general. So a believer should not speak loudly to the Prophet ﷺ as a slave speaks loudly to his master, otherwise he would have spoken loudly to him as one of you speaks loudly to another. One must not say: what is understood from this pattern is that you should not treat him as happens among yourselves, but rather distinguish him by not speaking loudly in his presence at all, while among yourselves you do not maintain reverence. For we say: what we have mentioned is closer to the reality, and it contains what you have mentioned of meaning plus more. What we have said is supported by the saying of the Exalted: ﴿The Prophet is closer to the believers than their own selves﴾ [al-Ahzab: 6]. A master is not closer to his slave than his own self, to the extent that if both were in famine and the slave found something which, if he did not eat it, he would die, he is not obligated to give it up to his master. Yet giving it up to the Prophet ﷺ is obligatory. And if the slave knew that by his death his master would be saved, he is not required to cast himself into destruction to save his master. Yet it is obligatory to save the Prophet, upon him be prayer and peace. We have already mentioned its reality in the commentary on the verse, and that wisdom requires this, just as the principal organ deserves more care than others, for when the heart is disordered, for example, the hands and feet no longer retain their soundness. So if a person preserved himself and abandoned the Prophet, upon him be prayer and peace, he would perish too, unlike the slave and master.

The second benefit: since the saying of the Exalted, ﴿do not raise your voices﴾, is of the same kind as ﴿do not speak loudly﴾, the call was not renewed. And since the former differs from the preceding [clause] in that one is an act and the other a speech, the call was renewed, as in Luqman's saying: ﴿O my son, do not associate﴾ [Luqman: 13], and his saying: ﴿O my son, establish prayer﴾ [Luqman: 17], because the first is an act of the heart and the second an act of the limbs. And [there is] his saying: ﴿O my son, establish prayer, enjoin what is right, and forbid what is wrong﴾ [Luqman: 17], without renewing the call, because all of these are acts of the limbs.

Know that if we say that the intended meaning of ﴿do not raise your voices﴾ is: do not speak excessively, then His saying ﴿and do not speak loudly﴾ will be a metaphor for bringing speech to the Prophet ﷺ only to the extent that it is brought to others; that is, do not speak much, and minimize speech to the utmost minimum. Likewise, if we say that the intended meaning of raising is address, then the intended meaning of ﴿do not speak loudly﴾ is: do not address him as you address others. The saying of the Exalted, ﴿lest your deeds become worthless﴾, has two well-known aspects:

One of them: "lest they become worthless."

The second: "for fear that they become worthless." We have mentioned this in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Allah makes clear to you, lest you go astray﴾ [al-Nisa: 176] and similar [verses]. It admits here of another aspect, which is to say its meaning is: fear Allah and avoid that your deeds become worthless. The evidence for this is that since the implicit element could not be avoided, what the speech in which it occurs indicates is more appropriate to be implied, and the command to piety has already preceded in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿and fear Allah﴾. As for the meaning, we say: the saying ﴿lest it become worthless﴾ is an indication that if you raise your voices and put yourselves forward, these vices will take root in you and lead to contempt, and that this leads to separation and apostasy that nullifies [deeds]. The saying of the Exalted, ﴿while you do not perceive﴾, is an indication that apostasy takes root in the self in such a way that a person does not perceive it. For whoever commits a sin he has never committed in his life, you see him extremely regretful and extremely fearful. But when he commits it repeatedly, the fear and regret diminish and it becomes a habit, without his knowing that it has taken root. This is the case whether it takes root in the first, second, third, or some other time. This is like one who receives a report: he does not affirm the word of the informant the first time. But when it is repeated to him and reaches the level of *tawatur* (mass transmission, i.e., reports so numerous as to yield certainty), certainty arises in him and belief becomes firmly established, and he does not know when that happened, or at which report this certainty arose. So the saying ﴿while you do not perceive﴾ is an emphasis of the prohibition, i.e., do not say that one time is excused and does not require retracting it, for the matter is not known. So close the door. There is another explanation in this: when the legally accountable person does not show reverence to the Prophet ﷺ and does not make himself like him in what he does on the basis of his command, he will be doing what he does on the basis of his own command. But what the self commands does not earn reward, and it is nullifying and nullified. Likewise, what he does without the command of the Prophet ﷺ is then nullified and nullifying. And Allah knows best.

Know that when Allah the Exalted commanded the believers to show reverence to the Prophet ﷺ, to honor him, and to give him precedence over themselves and over everything Allah has created, He commanded His Prophet, upon him be peace, to be gentle and merciful, and to be more compassionate to them than a parent, as He said: ﴿And lower your wing to the believers﴾ [al-Hijr: 88]. And the Exalted said: ﴿And keep yourself patient with those who call upon their Lord﴾ [al-Kahf: 28], and said: ﴿And do not be like the companion of the fish﴾ [al-Qalam: 48], and other such verses, so that his service would not be the service of tyrants who enslave free people by force, but rather their submission would be for the sake of the face of Allah.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, those who lower their voices in the presence of the Messenger of God, those are the ones whose hearts God has tested for piety.﴾

In this there is an exhortation to what He guided them to, from two aspects.

The first is evident to everyone, and it is in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿God has tested their hearts for piety.﴾ Its explanation is that whoever puts himself forward and raises his voice wants to honor himself and to be respected as a person. God, exalted is He, said: abandoning this self-regard is what brings about true respect, and by turning away from this self-honoring, honor is perfected, because through it your piety becomes manifest. And ﴿Indeed the most honorable of you in the sight of God is the most pious of you﴾ [al-Hujurat: 13]. It is shameful for a person to enter a bathhouse and choose a prominent place for himself there, thereby losing his standing with the ruler, and to magnify himself in the latrine and the resting place, and by that to become despised in a great gathering.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿God has tested their hearts for piety⦆ has several meanings:

The first: He tested them in order to know piety from them. Whoever magnifies one of the sons of his own kind because he is a sent messenger, his magnification of the one who sent him will be greater and his fear of Him stronger. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever magnifies the rites of God, indeed it is from the piety of hearts﴾ [al-Hajj: 32], that is, magnifying the commands of God is from the piety of God; likewise, magnifying the Messenger of God is from piety toward Him.

The second: "tested" means "knew and recognized," because testing is the recognition of a thing, so it is permissible to use it in that sense. On this view, the preposition "lām" (for) is attached to an omitted element, whose estimate is: God recognized their hearts as fit, that is, suitable for piety, just as a speaker says, "You are for such-and-such," meaning "you are fit for it" or "you are suited to it."

The third: "tested" means "purified," as it is said of gold: "tested" (mumtahan), that is, refined in the fire. All these meanings are mentioned. It is also possible to say that its meaning is: He tested them for piety, with the "lām" indicating causation. This may carry two senses:

The first: that it is a causal clause functioning as an explanation of a preceding cause, as a speaker says, "I came to you because of your honoring me yesterday," meaning that the earlier honoring became the cause of the coming.

The second: that it is a causal clause functioning as an explanation of an intended final purpose that is anticipated and comes afterward, not before, as a speaker says, "I came to you to perform a duty."

If we take the first view, its realization is that God knew the piety in their hearts and tested their hearts for the piety that was in them. Had their hearts not been filled with piety, He would not have commanded them to magnify His Messenger and to put His Prophet before themselves; rather, He would have said to them: "Believe in My Messenger, do not harm him, and do not deny him." For the unbeliever, the first thing he does in faith is acknowledge that the Prophet (ﷺ) is truthful. There is a great difference between one who is told, "Do not mock the Messenger of God, do not deny him, and do not harm him," and one who is told, "Do not raise your voice in his presence, do not give yourself any weight before him, and do not speak your truthful words loudly before him."

Know that to the degree that you put the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, before yourself in this world, to that same degree the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, will put you before himself in the hereafter, for no one will enter Paradise until God admits his community of the pious into Paradise.

If we take the second view, its realization is that God, exalted is He, tested their hearts through their knowledge of Him and of His Messenger with piety, that is, so that God would grant them the piety that is due to God in its full right (ḥaqq al-tuqāh), which is the piety that fears no one alongside the fear of God. Thus you see him secure from every frightening thing; he fears no loss in this world and no misfortune in the hereafter. The intelligent observer, when he knows that by fearing the ruler one is safe from the tyranny of the servants, and by avoiding the base people one is saved from the might of the ruler, makes the fear of the ruler a shield. Likewise, the scholar, if he reflects deeply, will know that through the fear of God comes salvation in both abodes, and through fear of other than Him comes ruin in both. So he makes the fear of God his shield, through which he finds himself safe in this world and the next.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿For them is forgiveness and a great reward.﴾

We have mentioned that forgiveness is the removal of the evil deeds that cling to the soul in this world, while the great reward is an allusion to the life that comes after the soul's separation from this world. God removes from him the bestial vices and clothes him in the angelic virtues.

﴿Indeed, those who call out to you from behind the apartments, most of them do not reason.﴾

This is an explanation of the state of those who stand in contrast to those mentioned before. The first lowered his voice, while the second raised it. In this there is an indication that it is an abandonment of the courtesy of being in his presence and presenting one's need to him. As for a person's saying to the king, "O So-and-so," it is a breach of courtesy. If you say: everyone says "O God" (yā Allāh), even though God is greater, we respond: calling out is of two kinds. One is to alert the one being called; the other is to make manifest the caller's need. An example of the first is a person saying to his companion or his servant, "O So-and-so." An example of the second is a person's saying in the nudba (the lamentation form of address, used in wailing): "O Commander of the Faithful, alas!" (yā amīra l-mu'minīnāh) or "O Zayd, alas!" (yā Zaydāh). Someone might say: if Zayd is in the east, there can be no alerting him, so how can one call out to him when he is dead? We respond: our saying "O God" is to make manifest the need of souls, not to alert the one called. Both aspects are present in calling out, because the caller calls only out of a need in himself which he presents, and in most cases he calls only when he is heedless or inattentive. Thus both aspects are present in calling. Their calling out was for alerting, and that is a breach of courtesy. As for one of us saying to a great man, "O my master" or "O my lord," it functions as description and information.

The second: the calling is from behind the apartments. Whoever calls to another with no barrier between them does not burden him with walking and coming; rather, he answers him from his place and speaks with him, and the caller seeks only that the one called turn his attention to him. Whoever calls to another from behind a barrier seems to want his presence, like one who calls to the owner of a garden from outside the garden.

The third: His saying ﴿the apartments﴾ is an allusion to the Prophet's (ﷺ) seclusion, in which it is not proper, in terms of courtesy, to come to him with a need at that time; rather, it is better to delay, even if the person is in a difficult need. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿most of them do not reason⦆ contains a declaration of their faults in proportion to the vices in their bad manners. This is because speech is one of the distinctive qualities of the human being, which is higher in rank than others, and those below him have no speech. But calling, in meaning, is like alerting, and it may occur through a sound produced when one thing strikes another. Among the dumb animals there is what is clearly manifest to everyone as calling: the ewe cries out and seeks its young, and so do other animals, and so does the young goat. So it is as if the calling took place in meaning for non-human beings. Thus God, exalted is He, said about them: ﴿most of them do not reason⦆, meaning: their calling, since it was not accompanied by good manners, placed them outside the rank of those who reason, and their calling was like the cry issuing from some animal.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿most (akthar) of them﴾ has two meanings:

The first: The Arabs mention "most" while intending "all," and they use "most" only out of caution to avoid lying and as a precaution in speech, because lying is something by which a person's deeds may be nullified in some matters. So he says "most," while in his belief it is "all." Then God, exalted is He, even with the full comprehensiveness of His knowledge of things, used language that suits their speech, and in this there is an allusion to a subtle point: God, exalted is He, says: "Even though My knowledge encompasses everything, I have followed your custom out of approval of that custom, which is avoiding lying. So do not abandon it, and take My choice of that in My speech as a decisive proof of My pleasure with it."

The second: The intended meaning is that they, in most of their states, do not reason. The realization of this is that when a person considers something with one attribute, and then considers it with another attribute, the first combined whole is not the second combined whole. An example: a person may be ignorant and poor, then become knowledgeable and wealthy; so people say in common usage, "Zayd is not the one I saw before; rather, now he is in the best condition," treating him as though he were not that person. This is an indication of what we have mentioned. Once this is understood: they, in some states, when you consider them with that state, are different from themselves when you consider them with another. So God said "most of them" as an allusion to what we have mentioned.

There is a third meaning as well, which is that one may say: perhaps among them are some who turned back from those desires, and among them are some who persisted in that bad custom. So He said "most of them," excluding those among them who repented.

The first: that it is a causal clause functioning as an explanation of a preceding cause, as a speaker says, "I came to you because of your honoring me yesterday," meaning that the earlier honoring became the cause of the coming.

The second: that it is a causal clause functioning as an explanation of an intended final purpose that is anticipated and comes afterward, not before, as a speaker says, "I came to you to perform a duty."

If we take the first view, its realization is that God knew the piety in their hearts and tested their hearts for the piety that was in them. Had their hearts not been filled with piety, He would not have commanded them to magnify His Messenger and to put His Prophet before themselves; rather, He would have said to them: "Believe in My Messenger, do not harm him, and do not deny him." For the unbeliever, the first thing he does in faith is acknowledge that the Prophet (ﷺ) is truthful. There is a great difference between one who is told, "Do not mock the Messenger of God, do not deny him, and do not harm him," and one who is told, "Do not raise your voice in his presence, do not give yourself any weight before him, and do not speak your truthful words loudly before him."

Know that to the degree that you put the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, before yourself in this world, to that same degree the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, will put you before himself in the hereafter, for no one will enter Paradise until God admits his community of the pious into Paradise.

If we take the second view, its realization is that God, exalted is He, tested their hearts through their knowledge of Him and of His Messenger with piety, that is, so that God would grant them the piety that is due to God in its full right (ḥaqq al-tuqāh), which is the piety that fears no one alongside the fear of God. Thus you see him secure from every frightening thing; he fears no loss in this world and no misfortune in the hereafter. The intelligent observer, when he knows that by fearing the ruler one is safe from the tyranny of the servants, and by avoiding the base people one is saved from the might of the ruler, makes the fear of the ruler a shield. Likewise, the scholar, if he reflects deeply, will know that through the fear of God comes salvation in both abodes, and through fear of other than Him comes ruin in both. So he makes the fear of God his shield, through which he finds himself safe in this world and the next.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿For them is forgiveness and a great reward.﴾

We have mentioned that forgiveness is the removal of the evil deeds that cling to the soul in this world, while the great reward is an allusion to the life that comes after the soul's separation from this world. God removes from him the bestial vices and clothes him in the angelic virtues.

﴿Indeed, those who call out to you from behind the apartments, most of them do not reason.﴾

This is an explanation of the state of those who stand in contrast to those mentioned before. The first lowered his voice, while the second raised it. In this there is an indication that it is an abandonment of the courtesy of being in his presence and presenting one's need to him. As for a person's saying to the king, "O So-and-so," it is a breach of courtesy. If you say: everyone says "O God" (yā Allāh), even though God is greater, we respond: calling out is of two kinds. One is to alert the one being called; the other is to make manifest the caller's need. An example of the first is a person saying to his companion or his servant, "O So-and-so." An example of the second is a person's saying in the nudba (the lamentation form of address, used in wailing): "O Commander of the Faithful, alas!" (yā amīra l-mu'minīnāh) or "O Zayd, alas!" (yā Zaydāh). Someone might say: if Zayd is in the east, there can be no alerting him, so how can one call out to him when he is dead? We respond: our saying "O God" is to make manifest the need of souls, not to alert the one called. Both aspects are present in calling out, because the caller calls only out of a need in himself which he presents, and in most cases he calls only when he is heedless or inattentive. Thus both aspects are present in calling. Their calling out was for alerting, and that is a breach of courtesy. As for one of us saying to a great man, "O my master" or "O my lord," it functions as description and information.

The second: the calling is from behind the apartments. Whoever calls to another with no barrier between them does not burden him with walking and coming; rather, he answers him from his place and speaks with him, and the caller seeks only that the one called turn his attention to him. Whoever calls to another from behind a barrier seems to want his presence, like one who calls to the owner of a garden from outside the garden.

The third: His saying ﴿the apartments﴾ is an allusion to the Prophet's (ﷺ) seclusion, in which it is not proper, in terms of courtesy, to come to him with a need at that time; rather, it is better to delay, even if the person is in a difficult need. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿most of them do not reason⦆ contains a declaration of their faults in proportion to the vices in their bad manners. This is because speech is one of the distinctive qualities of the human being, which is higher in rank than others, and those below him have no speech. But calling, in meaning, is like alerting, and it may occur through a sound produced when one thing strikes another. Among the dumb animals there is what is clearly manifest to everyone as calling: the ewe cries out and seeks its young, and so do other animals, and so does the young goat. So it is as if the calling took place in meaning for non-human beings. Thus God, exalted is He, said about them: ﴿most of them do not reason⦆, meaning: their calling, since it was not accompanied by good manners, placed them outside the rank of those who reason, and their calling was like the cry issuing from some animal.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿most (akthar) of them﴾ has two meanings:

The first: The Arabs mention "most" while intending "all," and they use "most" only out of caution to avoid lying and as a precaution in speech, because lying is something by which a person's deeds may be nullified in some matters. So he says "most," while in his belief it is "all." Then God, exalted is He, even with the full comprehensiveness of His knowledge of things, used language that suits their speech, and in this there is an allusion to a subtle point: God, exalted is He, says: "Even though My knowledge encompasses everything, I have followed your custom out of approval of that custom, which is avoiding lying. So do not abandon it, and take My choice of that in My speech as a decisive proof of My pleasure with it."

The second: The intended meaning is that they, in most of their states, do not reason. The realization of this is that when a person considers something with one attribute, and then considers it with another attribute, the first combined whole is not the second combined whole. An example: a person may be ignorant and poor, then become knowledgeable and wealthy; so people say in common usage, "Zayd is not the one I saw before; rather, now he is in the best condition," treating him as though he were not that person. This is an indication of what we have mentioned. Once this is understood: they, in some states, when you consider them with that state, are different from themselves when you consider them with another. So God said "most of them" as an allusion to what we have mentioned.

There is a third meaning as well, which is that one may say: perhaps among them are some who turned back from those desires, and among them are some who persisted in that bad custom. So He said "most of them," excluding those among them who repented.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if they had patiently waited until you came out to them, it would have been better for them﴾. This is an indication of the good manners opposite to the bad manners they displayed. For if they had been patient, they would not have needed to call out. And when you are coming out to them, it is not proper for them to come to them at a time when you are alone with yourself, or with your family, or with your Lord, for the self has its right and the family has its right. As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿it would have been better for them﴾, it may have two meanings:

The first: that what is intended is that this is the good and the better course, like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿better as an abode﴾ [al-Furqan: 24].

The second: that what is intended is that by calling out and not being patient they gain the immediate settling of their need and the relief of their want in the moment, and this is desirable, but safeguarding the Prophet ﷺ and honouring him is better than that, because it averts the essential need which is in the Hereafter, whereas the needs of this world are secondary. The nominative noun that the word "kāna" (it was) requires is either the patience, its implied sense being: if they had been patient, patience would have been better; or the coming out without calling, its implied sense being: if they had been patient until you came out to them, your coming out without being called would have been better for them. This suits the narration, because they asked him, upon him be blessings and peace, to come out so that they might take back their offspring; he came out and freed half of them, and they took the other half. Had they been patient, all of them would have been freed. The first meaning is more sound.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And God is Forgiving, Merciful﴾, confirming two matters. The first: the evil of their conduct in hastening. For when a person commits an ugly act and the king or master does not punish him, it is said: "How forbearing his master is," not to explain his forbearance, but to explain the great offence of the slave. The second: for the goodness of patience, meaning, by means of their doing what is better, God forgives them their misdeeds and makes this good deed an expiation for many misdeeds, just as it is said to a runaway slave who returns to his master's door: "You did well in your return, and your master is merciful," meaning that he will not punish you for what preceded of your sin because of the good deed you have done. It is possible to say that this is an exhortation to the Prophet ﷺ to pardon, and His saying, exalted is He, ﴿most of them do not understand﴾ serves as an excuse for them. We have mentioned that God, exalted is He, in some places mentions forgiveness before mercy, as in this surah, and mentions mercy before forgiveness in Surat Saba' in His saying: ﴿And He is the Merciful, the Forgiving﴾ [Saba': 2]. So where He says "Forgiving, Merciful," it means: He forgives his misdeeds, then looks upon him and sees him naked and in need, so He shows him mercy and clothes him in the garb of honour; and at times He sees him submerged in misdeeds, so He forgives his misdeeds, then shows him mercy after forgiveness. Sometimes the reference is to the mercy that follows forgiveness, so He mentions forgiveness first; and sometimes the mercy is before forgiveness, so He places it later. And since mercy is broad, existing both before forgiveness and after it, He mentions it both before and after.

This is of the utmost excellence in ordering. We say: God placed first what is most important over what is less, so He mentioned the side of God, then mentioned the side of the Messenger, then mentioned what leads to fighting among the groups of Muslims through listening to the words of the deviator and relying upon him, for it mentions everything that is most repellent to hearts. As for the present or absent believer, he does not harm a believer to a degree that leads to killing. Do you not see that God, exalted is He, mentioned, following the report of the deviator, the verse of fighting, saying: ﴿And if two groups of the believers fight﴾.

In the exegesis there are several issues:

First issue: concerning the occasion of revelation of this verse: the Prophet ﷺ sent al-Walid ibn Uqba, who was the half-brother of Uthman through their mother, as a collector and tax-agent to Banu al-Mustaliq, and they met him, but he thought they were fighters, so he returned to the Prophet ﷺ and said: "They refused and withheld." The Messenger ﷺ resolved to attack them, then this verse was revealed, and the Prophet ﷺ was informed that they had done none of that. This is good if they say the verse was revealed at that time; but if they say it was revealed specifically for that and limited to it, then no. Rather we say it was revealed in general, to show the necessity of verification and of not relying on the word of the deviator. What indicates the weakness of the view of those who say it was revealed for such and such is that God, exalted is He, did not say: "I revealed it for such and such," and it is not reported from the Prophet ﷺ that he explained that the verse came only for that. The utmost that can be said is that it was revealed at that time, and that is like a date for the revelation of the verse, and we affirm that. What confirms what we have mentioned is that applying the term "deviator" to al-Walid is a remote matter, for he was mistaken and assumed wrongly, and one who errs is not called a deviator. And how so, when in most contexts "deviator" refers to one who has left the bond of faith, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed God does not guide the deviant people﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 6], and His saying: ﴿so he deviated from the command of his Lord﴾ [al-Kahf: 50], and His saying: ﴿And as for those who deviated, their refuge is the Fire; whenever they wish to get out of it, they will be returned into it﴾ [as-Sajdah: 20], and so on.

Second issue: His saying: ﴿if a deviator comes to you with a report﴾ is an indication of a subtle point: the believer is described as being harsh upon the disbelievers and stern against them, so the deviator is not able to bring him a report, and if he is able to, it is rare. Thus He said: ﴿if he comes to you﴾ with the conditional particle, which is only mentioned together with expectation, since it is not good to say: "if the unripe date reddens," or "if the sun rises."

Third issue: an indefinite noun in a conditional context generalizes when it is in an affirmative setting, just as it generalizes in an informative statement when it is in a negative setting; and it specifies in a conditional context when it is in a negative setting, just as it specifies in an informative statement when it is in an affirmative setting. So let us mention its explanation by example and its proof. As for its explanation by example, we say: if someone says to his slave, "If I speak to a man, you are free," it is as if he said: "I will not speak to a man until the slave is freed by the speech of every man." And if he says: "If I do not speak to a man today, you are free," it is as if he said: "I will not speak to a man today until the slave is not freed by abstaining from speaking to every man," just as the oath does not become manifest in his speech by speaking to every man if he abstains from speaking to one man. As for the proof: the consideration is first to the affirmative side. Do you not see that without the particle "lam" (the negation particle), the positive is the basic form, and the negation requires a particle? The statement of the speaker, "Zayd is standing," was formulated first and did not require adding a particle to indicate the standing's affirmation for Zayd; whereas in the negative we need to say "Zayd is not standing." Had the original formulation and structure been for the negative, we would not have needed the extra particle for brevity or abbreviation. Given this, the statement "I saw a man" is satisfied by what makes it correct, namely seeing one person. But when you say "I did not see a man," it was formulated to oppose the statement "I saw a man," and was composed for that opposition, and opposites ought not both be true. So if the statement "I did not see a man" were satisfied by the non-seeing of more than one, then "I saw a man" and "I did not see a man" would both be true and would not be opposites; this obliges us, from the first convention, the second convention, and the generality in the negative side follows. Having understood this, we say: the conditional was formulated first, then composed after the categorical, as evidenced by the addition of the particle which stands in opposition to the categorical. And the speaker's statement, "If you are not free, I will not speak to a man," returns to the sense of negation. And just as the generality of the statement regarding the deviator is known, its generality regarding the report is known. So its meaning: whatever deviator comes to you with whatever report, verification of it is obligatory.

Fourth issue: the proof of our companions that the report of a single narrator is authoritative, and that the testimony of a deviator is not accepted. As for the first issue, they said: He grounded the command to suspend judgment on his being a deviator; and if the report of a single trustworthy narrator were not accepted, there would be no purpose in attaching the ruling to the deviator, and this is an argument from the concept (mafhum). As for the second, there are two reasons:

One: He commanded verification; so if He accepted his statement, the judge would not be commanded to verify, and the statement of the deviator would not be accepted. Moreover, God, exalted is He, commanded verification in the matter of report and news, and the domain of testimony is narrower than the domain of report.

The second: He, exalted is He, said: ﴿lest you harm a people in ignorance﴾, and ignorance is beyond error, for a mujtahid who errs is not called ignorant. Whoever bases a ruling on the word of a deviator, if he is not correct, has acted in ignorance, so building upon his statement is not permissible.

Fifth issue: ﴿an tuṣībū﴾ (lest you harm). We have mentioned two views concerning it. One of them is the view of the Kufans, namely that the intended meaning is "lest you harm."

Secondly: the view of the Basran (al-Basriyyun, the grammarians of Basra), which is that the intended meaning is "lest you dislike that you should afflict." It is also possible to say that the intended meaning is: "investigate, and fear God." His words, ﴿lest you afflict a people﴾, clarify what we mentioned: the wrongdoer (al-fasiq) may say that strife appears among peoples. This is not the case with harmful words spoken to a person's face, or with backbiting (al-ghibah) issued by believers, because a believer's religion prevents him from vulgarity and from exaggerating in causing distress. His words, ﴿in ignorance﴾, are in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: lest you afflict them while you are ignorant. There is a subtle point here: the verb "to afflict" (al-isabah) is used for both bad and good, as in His words, ﴿Whatever good befalls you is from God﴾ [al-Nisa larly: 79]. However, it is used mostly for what is harmful, but the evil assumption (al-zann al-su') is mentioned along with it, as in His words, ﴿And if an evil befalls them﴾ [al-Shura: 48]. Then He confirmed this with His words, ﴿then you will become, regarding what you have done, regretful﴾, clarifying that the one who is ignorant must necessarily be regretful for his deed. His words, ﴿fa-tusbihu﴾, mean "you will become," and the grammarians said: asbaha (to become/be in the morning) is used in three ways:

First: in the sense of a man entering the morning, as when one says: "We woke up (asbahna) judging against him."

Second: in the sense of "the matter was, at the time of morning, such and such," as when one says: "Our patient became (asbaha) better today than he was, but he deteriorated at mid-morning," meaning that he was better at the time of dawn, and his state changed by midday.

Third: in the sense of "became (sara)," as when one says: "Zayd became (asbaha) rich," meaning he became so without intending a particular time over another. The meaning intended here is the third meaning, and likewise amsa and adha. However, there is a verification of this: we say that difference in words requires difference in meanings and difference in benefits. So we say: becoming (al-sayrurah) may be from the beginning of a matter and continue, it may be at its end in the sense of "the matter reached that," and it may be intermediate.

Example of the first: the saying of one who says: "The child became (sara) understanding," meaning he began to understand and is increasing in it.

Example of the second: the saying of one who says: "The truth became (sara) clear and obligatory," meaning its limit ended and it took its due.

Example of the third: the saying of one who says: "Zayd became (sara) knowledgeable and strong," when he does not intend that he has begun it or reached its end, but rather that he is clothed in it and characterized by it.

Once you know this, the root use of asbaha is for when a thing becomes one who has begun a quality and started a matter; the root use of amsa is for when a thing becomes one who has reached the extreme of the quality; and the root use of adha is intermediacy. It cannot be said: "The users of the language do not distinguish between matters and use the three words with one meaning." We say: when meanings are close, the usage is permitted, and permissibility of usage does not contradict the root. Many words have as their root a past sense but are commonly used for what does not share it. Once this is known, we say: His words, ﴿fa-tusbihu﴾, mean: "so you will become (sara) those who have begun regret and are clothed in it, then you will persist in it." Likewise in His words, ﴿fa-asbahtum bi-ni'matihi ikhwanan﴾ [Al 'Imran: 103], meaning: you began brotherhood while you are increasing in it and persisting in it. In sum, He chose this word in the Qur'an because the matter associated with it is either in reward or in punishment, and both are in increase, [Page 105] and there is no end to divine matters.

His words, ﴿nadimin﴾ (regretful): regret (al-nadam) is a constant sorrow, and the letters nun, dal and mim in its permutations do not separate from the meaning of permanence, as in the saying of one who says: "He persisted (adman) in drinking," and "mudmin" means he remained. From this comes "al-Madinah" (the city).

His words, ﴿fa-tusbihu 'ala ma fa'altum nadimin﴾, contain two benefits:

The first: affirming and emphasizing the warning. Its aspect is that when He said, ﴿lest you afflict a people in ignorance﴾, He then said after it: this is not something to be disregarded, and it is not permissible for a sensible person to say, "Suppose I afflicted a people, what is it to me?" Rather, upon you from it is constant concern and lasting grief, and such a matter must be guarded against.

The second: praise of the believers, meaning: you are not among those who, when they commit an evil, do not give it any heed, but rather you become regretful for it.
