If it is said: why did he not mention the believer before the deviator, so that the ranks would be graded, beginning with God and His Messenger, then the present believer, then the absent believer, then the deviator? We say: God placed first what is most important over what is less, so He mentioned the side of God, then mentioned the side of the Messenger, then mentioned what leads to fighting among the groups of Muslims through listening to the words of the deviator and relying upon him, for it mentions everything that is most repellent to hearts. As for the present or absent believer, he does not harm a believer to a degree that leads to killing. Do you not see that God, exalted is He, mentioned, following the report of the deviator, the verse of fighting, saying: ﴿And if two groups of the believers fight﴾.

In the exegesis there are several issues:

First issue: concerning the occasion of revelation of this verse: the Prophet ﷺ sent al-Walid ibn Uqba, who was the half-brother of Uthman through their mother, as a collector and tax-agent to Banu al-Mustaliq, and they met him, but he thought they were fighters, so he returned to the Prophet ﷺ and said: "They refused and withheld." The Messenger ﷺ resolved to attack them, then this verse was revealed, and the Prophet ﷺ was informed that they had done none of that. This is good if they say the verse was revealed at that time; but if they say it was revealed specifically for that and limited to it, then no. Rather we say it was revealed in general, to show the necessity of verification and of not relying on the word of the deviator. What indicates the weakness of the view of those who say it was revealed for such and such is that God, exalted is He, did not say: "I revealed it for such and such," and it is not reported from the Prophet ﷺ that he explained that the verse came only for that. The utmost that can be said is that it was revealed at that time, and that is like a date for the revelation of the verse, and we affirm that. What confirms what we have mentioned is that applying the term "deviator" to al-Walid is a remote matter, for he was mistaken and assumed wrongly, and one who errs is not called a deviator. And how so, when in most contexts "deviator" refers to one who has left the bond of faith, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed God does not guide the deviant people﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 6], and His saying: ﴿so he deviated from the command of his Lord﴾ [al-Kahf: 50], and His saying: ﴿And as for those who deviated, their refuge is the Fire; whenever they wish to get out of it, they will be returned into it﴾ [as-Sajdah: 20], and so on.

Second issue: His saying: ﴿if a deviator comes to you with a report﴾ is an indication of a subtle point: the believer is described as being harsh upon the disbelievers and stern against them, so the deviator is not able to bring him a report, and if he is able to, it is rare. Thus He said: ﴿if he comes to you﴾ with the conditional particle, which is only mentioned together with expectation, since it is not good to say: "if the unripe date reddens," or "if the sun rises."

Third issue: an indefinite noun in a conditional context generalizes when it is in an affirmative setting, just as it generalizes in an informative statement when it is in a negative setting; and it specifies in a conditional context when it is in a negative setting, just as it specifies in an informative statement when it is in an affirmative setting. So let us mention its explanation by example and its proof. As for its explanation by example, we say: if someone says to his slave, "If I speak to a man, you are free," it is as if he said: "I will not speak to a man until the slave is freed by the speech of every man." And if he says: "If I do not speak to a man today, you are free," it is as if he said: "I will not speak to a man today until the slave is not freed by abstaining from speaking to every man," just as the oath does not become manifest in his speech by speaking to every man if he abstains from speaking to one man. As for the proof: the consideration is first to the affirmative side. Do you not see that without the particle "lam" (the negation particle), the positive is the basic form, and the negation requires a particle? The statement of the speaker, "Zayd is standing," was formulated first and did not require adding a particle to indicate the standing's affirmation for Zayd; whereas in the negative we need to say "Zayd is not standing." Had the original formulation and structure been for the negative, we would not have needed the extra particle for brevity or abbreviation. Given this, the statement "I saw a man" is satisfied by what makes it correct, namely seeing one person. But when you say "I did not see a man," it was formulated to oppose the statement "I saw a man," and was composed for that opposition, and opposites ought not both be true. So if the statement "I did not see a man" were satisfied by the non-seeing of more than one, then "I saw a man" and "I did not see a man" would both be true and would not be opposites; this obliges us, from the first convention, the second convention, and the generality in the negative side follows. Having understood this, we say: the conditional was formulated first, then composed after the categorical, as evidenced by the addition of the particle which stands in opposition to the categorical. And the speaker's statement, "If you are not free, I will not speak to a man," returns to the sense of negation. And just as the generality of the statement regarding the deviator is known, its generality regarding the report is known. So its meaning: whatever deviator comes to you with whatever report, verification of it is obligatory.

Fourth issue: the proof of our companions that the report of a single narrator is authoritative, and that the testimony of a deviator is not accepted. As for the first issue, they said: He grounded the command to suspend judgment on his being a deviator; and if the report of a single trustworthy narrator were not accepted, there would be no purpose in attaching the ruling to the deviator, and this is an argument from the concept (mafhum). As for the second, there are two reasons:

One: He commanded verification; so if He accepted his statement, the judge would not be commanded to verify, and the statement of the deviator would not be accepted. Moreover, God, exalted is He, commanded verification in the matter of report and news, and the domain of testimony is narrower than the domain of report.

The second: He, exalted is He, said: ﴿lest you harm a people in ignorance﴾, and ignorance is beyond error, for a mujtahid who errs is not called ignorant. Whoever bases a ruling on the word of a deviator, if he is not correct, has acted in ignorance, so building upon his statement is not permissible.

Fifth issue: ﴿an tuṣībū﴾ (lest you harm). We have mentioned two views concerning it. One of them is the view of the Kufans, namely that the intended meaning is "lest you harm."

Secondly: the view of the Basran (al-Basriyyun, the grammarians of Basra), which is that the intended meaning is "lest you dislike that you should afflict." It is also possible to say that the intended meaning is: "investigate, and fear God." His words, ﴿lest you afflict a people﴾, clarify what we mentioned: the wrongdoer (al-fasiq) may say that strife appears among peoples. This is not the case with harmful words spoken to a person's face, or with backbiting (al-ghibah) issued by believers, because a believer's religion prevents him from vulgarity and from exaggerating in causing distress. His words, ﴿in ignorance﴾, are in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: lest you afflict them while you are ignorant. There is a subtle point here: the verb "to afflict" (al-isabah) is used for both bad and good, as in His words, ﴿Whatever good befalls you is from God﴾ [al-Nisa larly: 79]. However, it is used mostly for what is harmful, but the evil assumption (al-zann al-su') is mentioned along with it, as in His words, ﴿And if an evil befalls them﴾ [al-Shura: 48]. Then He confirmed this with His words, ﴿then you will become, regarding what you have done, regretful﴾, clarifying that the one who is ignorant must necessarily be regretful for his deed. His words, ﴿fa-tusbihu﴾, mean "you will become," and the grammarians said: asbaha (to become/be in the morning) is used in three ways:

First: in the sense of a man entering the morning, as when one says: "We woke up (asbahna) judging against him."

Second: in the sense of "the matter was, at the time of morning, such and such," as when one says: "Our patient became (asbaha) better today than he was, but he deteriorated at mid-morning," meaning that he was better at the time of dawn, and his state changed by midday.

Third: in the sense of "became (sara)," as when one says: "Zayd became (asbaha) rich," meaning he became so without intending a particular time over another. The meaning intended here is the third meaning, and likewise amsa and adha. However, there is a verification of this: we say that difference in words requires difference in meanings and difference in benefits. So we say: becoming (al-sayrurah) may be from the beginning of a matter and continue, it may be at its end in the sense of "the matter reached that," and it may be intermediate.

Example of the first: the saying of one who says: "The child became (sara) understanding," meaning he began to understand and is increasing in it.

Example of the second: the saying of one who says: "The truth became (sara) clear and obligatory," meaning its limit ended and it took its due.

Example of the third: the saying of one who says: "Zayd became (sara) knowledgeable and strong," when he does not intend that he has begun it or reached its end, but rather that he is clothed in it and characterized by it.

Once you know this, the root use of asbaha is for when a thing becomes one who has begun a quality and started a matter; the root use of amsa is for when a thing becomes one who has reached the extreme of the quality; and the root use of adha is intermediacy. It cannot be said: "The users of the language do not distinguish between matters and use the three words with one meaning." We say: when meanings are close, the usage is permitted, and permissibility of usage does not contradict the root. Many words have as their root a past sense but are commonly used for what does not share it. Once this is known, we say: His words, ﴿fa-tusbihu﴾, mean: "so you will become (sara) those who have begun regret and are clothed in it, then you will persist in it." Likewise in His words, ﴿fa-asbahtum bi-ni'matihi ikhwanan﴾ [Al 'Imran: 103], meaning: you began brotherhood while you are increasing in it and persisting in it. In sum, He chose this word in the Qur'an because the matter associated with it is either in reward or in punishment, and both are in increase, [Page 105] and there is no end to divine matters.

His words, ﴿nadimin﴾ (regretful): regret (al-nadam) is a constant sorrow, and the letters nun, dal and mim in its permutations do not separate from the meaning of permanence, as in the saying of one who says: "He persisted (adman) in drinking," and "mudmin" means he remained. From this comes "al-Madinah" (the city).

His words, ﴿fa-tusbihu 'ala ma fa'altum nadimin﴾, contain two benefits:

The first: affirming and emphasizing the warning. Its aspect is that when He said, ﴿lest you afflict a people in ignorance﴾, He then said after it: this is not something to be disregarded, and it is not permissible for a sensible person to say, "Suppose I afflicted a people, what is it to me?" Rather, upon you from it is constant concern and lasting grief, and such a matter must be guarded against.

The second: praise of the believers, meaning: you are not among those who, when they commit an evil, do not give it any heed, but rather you become regretful for it.

[Page 105]

Then God the Exalted said: ﴿And know that among you is the Messenger of God. Were he to obey you in many matters, you would surely be in distress. But God has made faith beloved to you and has made it attractive in your hearts, and He has made disbelief, defiance and disobedience hateful to you.﴾

In explaining this verse, we will mention what has been said and what may be said. As for what has been said, we will choose the best of it, which is what al-Zamakhshari chose. He discussed the explanation of this verse at great length and said: God the Exalted's words ﴿Were he to obey you in many matters, you would surely be in distress﴾ are not a new independent statement, because that would lead to a disjointed composition, since there would be no connection between His words ﴿And know﴾ and His words ﴿Were he to obey you﴾. The correct connection is that His words ﴿Were he to obey you﴾ are in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to the nominative pronoun in His words "among you" (fīkum). The sense is: "[The Messenger of God] is present among you in a state in which you want him to obey you or to act according to your judgment. He should not be in that state, because if he did that, ﴿you would be in distress﴾, or you would fall into hardship, or you would be destroyed by it."

* * *

Then God the Exalted said: ﴿But God has made faith beloved to you﴾, addressing some of the believers who were not the ones addressed by His words ﴿Were he to obey you﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: He relied on the difference in the description and abbreviated, and did not say "He has made faith beloved to some of you." He also said that God's words ﴿Were he to obey you﴾ rather than "if he obeyed you" indicate that they wanted this state to continue, and that the Prophet (ﷺ) would continue to act according to their judgment. However, what follows it is in contrast to what precedes it, and here it is the same, even though the contrast is not stated explicitly, because the difference in the addressees in the description shows us this. The ones addressed first by His words ﴿Were he to obey you﴾ are those who wanted the Prophet (ﷺ) to act according to their desire, and the ones addressed by His words ﴿He has made faith beloved to you﴾ are those who wanted to act according to the desire of the Prophet (ﷺ). This is what al-Zamakhshari said and chose, and it is good. What may be said, and which is apparently the stronger view, is this: when God the Exalted said ﴿If a defiant one comes to you with news, then verify (tabayyanū)﴾, that is, be certain and investigate, He then said, ﴿And know that among you is the Messenger of God﴾, meaning: the investigation is easy for you by returning to the Prophet (ﷺ), for he is among you as a clarifier and a guide. This is like when someone, upon disagreement among the students of a teacher regarding a question, says: "This teacher is sitting here." He does not intend to state where he is sitting, but intends to order them to refer to him. That is because what is meant is that "he will not obey you in many matters." The teacher, in the example we mentioned,

[Page 106]

if he relied on the statements of the students, their hearts would not be reassured by returning to him. But if he mentions only sound transmission and establishes it with strong proof, everyone will refer to him. Likewise here, He said: "Seek his guidance, for he knows and obeys no one, so no bias is found in him and no falsehood is passed off upon him." What indicates that the meaning of God's words ﴿Were he to obey you in many matters, you would surely be in distress﴾ is a statement that he does not obey you, is that the conditional sentence (al-jumla al-shartiyya) in many contexts is used to show the impossibility of the condition because of the impossibility of the consequence, as in God's words ﴿Had there been in them (the heavens and the earth) gods other than God, they would both have been corrupted﴾ [al-Anbiyā’: 22], and His words ﴿Had it been from other than God, they would have found in it much discrepancy﴾ [al-Nisā’: 82]. This shows that there are not in them any gods, and that it is not from other than God.

* * *

Then God the Exalted said: ﴿But God has made faith beloved to you and made it attractive in your hearts﴾, as an indication of the answer to an objection that arises concerning His words ﴿then verify﴾. The objection is that someone might say: "There is no need to refer back, and our intellects are sufficient. By them we perceive faith and leave disobedience, and so we strive in our affairs." He answered: The perception of faith does not come through striving; rather, God has made clear the proof and made faith attractive, until certainty is attained, and after certainty is attained, it is not permissible to hesitate. God only commanded you to hesitate when accepting the report of a defiant one, and He did not command you to be stubborn after the proof has become clear. It is as if He said: "Hesitate concerning what is doubtful, but faith has been made beloved to you through proof, so do not hesitate to accept it." According to our view, the addressee of His words ﴿has made beloved to you﴾ is the addressee of His words ﴿Were he to obey you﴾. Now that you know the meaning of the verse as a whole, hear it in detail, and we will explain it in issues:

Issue One: If someone says: If the intent of His words ﴿And know that among you is the Messenger of God﴾ is to return to him and rely on his word, why did He not say explicitly "verify (tabayyanū) and refer to the Prophet (ﷺ)"? And what is the benefit of turning to this figurative usage (majāz, figurative usage)? We say: the benefit is an increase in emphasis. That is because the statement of the speaker in the example we mentioned, "This teacher is sitting here," is more emphatic regarding the obligation to refer to him than saying "refer to your teacher." That is because the speaker makes the obligation to refer to him something agreed upon, and makes the reason for not referring to him their lack of knowledge of his sitting. So it is as if he says: "You do not doubt that the one who reveals the truth is the teacher, and that it is obligatory to refer to him. If you do not know that he is sitting, then he is sitting." Thus he makes the goodness of referring to him more apparent than the matter of sitting. It is as if he says: "His sitting is hidden from you, so you have abandoned referring to him, but the goodness of referring to him is not hidden from you." So he makes the goodness of referring to him more apparent than the sensory matter. This differs from saying "refer to him," because then he would be saying: "You did not know that referring to him is the way." Between the two statements there is a great distance. Likewise, God's words ﴿And know that among you is the Messenger of God﴾ mean: "The obligation to refer to him is not hidden from you. If his presence among you was hidden from you, then know that he is among you." So He makes the goodness of referring to him more apparent than his being among them, since He left aside clarifying it and turned to explaining his presence among them. This is one of the precious meanings found in figurative usages (majāz) and not found in the explicit (ṣarīḥ) statement.

Issue Two: If the intent of His words ﴿Were he to obey you﴾ is to show that he does not obey anyone but follows revelation, why did He not state this explicitly? We say: stating the negation of a thing together with the proof of the negation is more complete than stating it without proof. The conditional sentence states the negation together with its proof. If someone says, "Why do you say that there are no gods in them?", one must mention the proof, so one says: ﴿Had there been in them gods other than God, they would both have been corrupted﴾ [al-Anbiyā’: 22]. Likewise here: if He had said "He does not obey you," and someone asked, "Why does he not obey?", it would have been necessary to say: "If he obeyed you, he would obey you for the sake of your benefit, but there is no benefit for you in it, because you would be in distress and sin, and it would grieve him that you are in hardship," as He said: ﴿It grieves him that you suffer hardship﴾ [al-Tawba: 128]. His obeying you would not benefit him in anything, so he does not obey you. This is the negation of obedience with proof, and there is a great difference between negating a thing with proof and negating it without proof.

Issue Three: He said ﴿in many matters﴾ so that it would be known that he may agree with them and act according to their benefit, realizing the purpose of His words ﴿and consult them in the matter﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 159].

Issue Four: If the intent of God's words ﴿has made faith beloved to you﴾ is "do not hesitate," why did He not state it explicitly? We say: because of what we have explained concerning the indication of the matter's clarity. That is, you know that certainty is not subject to hesitation, since there is no level beyond it at which one would hesitate until reaching it, because whoever reaches the level of conjecture (ẓann) hesitates until he reaches the level of certainty. Since the absence of hesitation in certainty is known and agreed upon, He did not say "so do not hesitate," but said ﴿has made faith beloved to you﴾, meaning: He made it clear and made it attractive by means of certain proof.

Issue Five: What is the meaning of His words ﴿has made faith beloved to you and made it attractive in your hearts﴾? We say: God's words ﴿has made beloved to you﴾ mean He brought it near and placed it in your hearts. Then He made it attractive within them so that you would not part from it, and it would not leave your hearts. This is because whoever loves things may tire of some of them when they are obtained and their stay is prolonged. Yet faith becomes more beautiful every day. But whoever's worship is greater and who endures the hardships of obligations more fully, worship and obligations become sweeter and more perfect for him. For this reason He said at first ﴿has made beloved to you﴾, and second ﴿and made it attractive in your hearts﴾, as if He brought it near to them and then established it in their hearts.

Issue Six: What is the difference between the three things: disbelief (kufr), defiance (fusūq), and disobedience (ʿiṣyān)? We say: these are three things in opposition to complete faith, because complete adorned faith is that which combines affirmation in the heart, declaration by the tongue, and action by the limbs:

The first: God's words ﴿and made disbelief hateful to you﴾, which is denial in opposition to affirmation by the heart. Defiance (fusūq) is lying.

The second: what precedes this verse, namely God's words ﴿If a defiant one comes to you with news﴾. He called the one who lies "defiant," so lying is defiance.

The third: what He mentioned after this verse, namely God's words ﴿Wretched is the name of defiance after faith﴾ [al-Ḥujurāt: 11]. This indicates that defiance is a verbal matter, because it is linked to the word "name." We will explain its interpretation, God willing.

The fourth: a rational point, which is that defiance is departure from obedience, as is known in the saying: "The date-palm shoot (rubaṭa) defied (fasaqat) when it came out," and other usages, because defiance is departure. Its usage has been extended to mean departure from obedience. But departure does not have a manifestation in the heart, since no one has knowledge of what is in hearts except God the Exalted, and it does not appear through actions, because a command may be neglected either through forgetfulness or inadvertence, so the state of the one who neglects or commits a transgression is not known as to whether he erred or did it deliberately. As for speech, it gives knowledge of the state of the speaker. Entering into faith and leaving it becomes apparent through speech, so restricting defiance to the verbal matter is closer. As for disobedience (ʿiṣyān), it is abandonment of a command, and this is more fitting in action. When this is known, there is an arrangement of great excellence in it: God made disbelief hateful to you, which is the greatest matter, as He said: ﴿Indeed, associating partners with God is a tremendous wrong﴾ [Luqmān: 13].

* * *

Then God the Exalted said: ﴿and defiance﴾, meaning what your tongues also manifest. Then He said: ﴿and disobedience﴾, which is less than all of these, and He did not leave aside the lesser matter, which is disobedience. Some people said: disbelief is evident, defiance is the major sin (kabīra), and disobedience is the minor sin (ṣaghīra). But what we have mentioned is stronger.

* * *

Then God the Exalted said: ﴿Those are the rightly guided﴾.

[Page 108]

This is an address to the Prophet (ﷺ), and in it there is a subtle meaning: at the beginning God the Exalted said: ﴿And know that among you is the Messenger of God﴾, meaning he is a guide for you. The address to the believers serves to draw attention to his compassion for the believers. He said at first: the Prophet is sufficient as a guide for you in what you seek guidance for, so he showed compassion to them and guided them. On this basis, His words ﴿the rightly guided﴾ mean: those who are conformed to rectitude (rushd), who take what comes to them and refrain from what he forbids them.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿As a bounty from God and a favour. And God is All-Knowing, All-Wise﴾. And in this there are several issues:

The first issue: fadlan (as a bounty) is in the accusative for several reasons. It may be in the accusative as a maf'ul lahu (object of purpose), and in this there are two views:

The first: the governing element (al-'amil) in it is the verb in His words: ﴿the rightly guided﴾. If it is said: how is it permissible for God's bounty, which is God's act, to be an object of purpose in relation to guidance, which is the servant's act? We say: since guidance is a granting of success from God, it is as if it were God's act. So it is as if He, exalted is He, guided them as a bounty, meaning that He is bestowing favour upon them and conferring benefit on their behalf.

The second view: the governing element is His saying: ﴿He has made faith beloved to you and has adorned it in your hearts, and has made disbelief, wickedness and rebellion hateful to you﴾ as a bounty, and His saying: ﴿those are the rightly guided﴾ is a parenthetical clause inserted between the two statements. Or the governing element is a supposed verb, as if He had said: that happened as a bounty from God. Or it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), and in this there are two views:

The first: that it is a masdar of a non-verbal kind (min ghayr al-lafz), and because guidance is a bounty, it is as if He had said: ﴿those are the rightly guided, a guidance﴾.

The second: that it is a masdar of a hidden verb, as if He had said: He made faith beloved to you and made disbelief hateful to you, so He bestowed a bounty and conferred a favour. The view that it is in the accusative as an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq), which is the masdar, or as an object of purpose, is the view of al-Zamakhshari. Or it may be that fadlan is a direct object (maf'ul bihi), with the verb hidden, indicated by His saying: ﴿those are the rightly guided﴾, meaning: they seek a bounty from God and a favour.

The second issue: What is the difference between fadl (bounty) and ni'mah (favour) in the verse? We say: God's fadl indicates the good that is with Him, of which He has no need, while ni'mah indicates what reaches the servant, and the servant is in need of it. For fadl in origin points to surplus, and with Him are treasuries of mercy, not because He needs them, and He sends down from them upon His servants what leaves them in no state of need in any way. And ni'mah points to tenderness and mercy, and it comes from the side of the servant. In this there is a subtle meaning, which is the emphasis on giving: the one in need says to the Rich: give me what is left over from you and what is with you; and that is not a matter for which account is taken, and it is what sustains my standing and my continuing. So His saying: ﴿a bounty from God﴾ indicates what comes from the side of God, the Rich, and ni'mah indicates what comes from the side of the servant, namely the removal of need. This is among what confirms our statement that fadlan is governed by a hidden verb, namely seeking and asking.

The third issue: the ending of the verse with His saying: ﴿And God is All-Knowing, All-Wise﴾. In this there are several connections. Among them: when God, exalted is He, mentioned the report of the wicked person, He said: if it should be confused for the believer whether the wicked person is lying, then do not rely on his deception that he presents falsehood to you, for God is All-Knowing; and do not say, as was the habit of the hypocrite: "Why does God not punish us for what we say?", for God is All-Wise, who does nothing except in accordance with His wisdom.

Second: when God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And know that among you is the Messenger of God; if he were to obey you﴾ in the sense of: he would not obey you, but follows the revelation, He said: for God, by His being All-Knowing, informs him, and by His being All-Wise, commands him with what wisdom requires, so follow him.

Third: the connection between His saying, exalted is He, "All-Knowing, All-Wise," and His saying: ﴿He has made faith beloved to you﴾, meaning: He made faith beloved to the people of faith by His knowledge, and chose for it whom He wills by His wisdom.

Fourth, and this is the closest: He, glorified and exalted, said: ﴿As a bounty from God and a favour﴾. Since fadl is the good that is with God, of which He has no need, He said: He is All-Knowing of what is in the treasuries of His mercy of good; and ni'mah is that which removes the servant's need. He said: He is All-Wise, who sends down good in the measure that He wills, in accordance with wisdom.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 49, verse 9–10 (part 1 of 2):

Then He, glorified and exalted, said: ﴿And if two groups of the believers fight, then make peace between them. But if one of them transgresses against the other, then fight against the one that transgresses until it returns to the command of Allah.﴾

When Allah warned the believers about the report brought by the corrupt person (al-fasiq), He pointed to what follows from it as a means of correcting what is lost. So He said: If it happens that you act upon the word of one who sows discord among you, and the matter leads to the fighting of two groups of the believers, then remove what that corrupt person has established and make peace between them. ﴿But if one of them transgresses against the other, then fight against the one that transgresses﴾, meaning the wrongdoer, whom it is obligatory upon you to repel from the other. For this reason, when a Muslim dies and has a disbelieving brother, his property goes to the Muslims and not to his disbelieving brother. As for the disbeliever...

so too, because in lineage the relevant father is the one who is a father in the sacred law (shar'an). Indeed the offspring of fornication from one man do not inherit from each other. Likewise disbelief is like an invalid intercourse, and it is like an incapable intercourse that does not produce brotherhood. For this reason, whoever dies in disbelief, having a Muslim brother but no heir by lineage, his property is not given to the disbelievers. Had religion gathered them, the property of an unbeliever would go to the unbelievers, just as the property of a Muslim goes to the Muslims when there is no heir.

If it is said: It has been established that brotherhood by Islam is stronger than brotherhood by lineage, as evidenced by the fact that a Muslim is inherited from by Muslims, and a disbelieving brother by lineage does not inherit from him. Why, then, did they not give precedence to Islamic brotherhood over lineal brotherhood absolutely, so that the property of a Muslim goes to the Muslims and not to his brothers by lineage?

We say: This is a corrupt question. Because a Muslim brother who is also a brother by lineage has two brotherhoods united in him, so he becomes stronger, and agnatic priority belongs to the one who has the greater strength. Do you not see that a full brother (from both parents) inherits, while a half brother (from the father) does not inherit alongside him? Likewise, a Muslim who is a brother by lineage has two brotherhoods, so he is given precedence over all other Muslims. And God knows best.

The fourth issue: The grammarians said: "mā" in this position is a *kāffah* (a particle that "restrains," i.e., the particle that removes the governing power of a word, here "inna," which cancels its operation), restraining "inna" from its operation. Were it not so, one would say: *innamā al-mu'minūna ikhwatun* with "inna" in its governing role. In His words, ﴿So by a mercy from God﴾ [Al 'Imran: 159] and His words ﴿after a little﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 40], it is not *kāffah*. The stronger question is that *rubba*, the prepositions *bi* and *'an*, are like this, and the "mā" in *rubba* is *kāffah*, while in *'ammā* and *bimā* it is not *kāffah*. The verification of this is that the speech after *rubbamā* is complete and can be made independent; if you omitted *rubbamā* and *innamā*, it would do no harm. So we say: *rubbamā qāma al-amīru* and *rubbamā Zayd fī al-dār*. If you omitted *rubbamā* and said "Zayd is in the house and the commander stood," it would be valid. The same applies to *innamā* and *lakinnamā*. As for *'ammā* and *bimā*, they are not like this; because His words ﴿So by a mercy from God you were gentle with them﴾ [Al 'Imran: 159], if you removed *bimā* and said "a mercy from God, you were gentle with them," it would not be a complete utterance. The *bi* is considered to have its attachment to what it needs, so it remains in effect in reality, whereas with *lakinnamā*, *innamā* and *rubbamā*, since they have been dispensed with, it is as if their ruling has not remained and they have no governing effect on what is no longer there. If it is said: when *inna* is not restrained by *mā*, what follows it is a complete utterance, so it should have no governing effect. You say: "Inna Zayd qā'imun"; if you said "Zayd qā'imun" it would suffice and be complete? We say: That is not so, because what follows *inna* may be indefinite. You say: "Inna rajulan jā'anī wa-akhbarānī bi-kadhā wa-akhbarānī bi-'aksihi," and you say "jā'anī rajulun wa-akhbarānī," and it is not good to say "innamā rajulun jā'anī" as if *innamā* were not there. The same applies to *baynamā* and *aynamā*: if you removed them and confined yourself to what follows them, it would not be complete, so it was not restrained. The discussion of *la'alla* has been mentioned repeatedly before.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿O you who believe, let not a people ridicule another people, perhaps they may be better than them; nor let women ridicule other women, perhaps they may be better than them; and do not defame one another, nor call one another by offensive nicknames﴾.

We have already explained that the surah is guidance following guidance. After guidance on what the believer should be toward Allah the Exalted, toward the Prophet (ﷺ), and toward one who opposes and disobeys them, namely the wicked person (fasiq), He explained what the believer should be toward fellow believers.

Page 113

We have mentioned that a believer is either present or absent. If he is present, he should not be ridiculed, nor should attention be paid to him in a way that contradicts honoring him. In the verse there is an indication to three matters arranged in order, one below the other: sukhriyyah (ridicule), lamz (defamation), and nabz (offensive naming). Sukhriyyah is that a person does not look at his brother with an eye of reverence, does not regard him, and brings him down from his rank; and then he does not mention his good qualities. This is like what some people said: "When their enemy is mentioned in their presence, they say: he is too insignificant to be mentioned, and less than to be given any attention." So He said: "Do not belittle your brothers or consider them insignificant."

The second is lamz, which is mentioning a man's faults in his absence. This is lower than the first, because in the first the person is not even given attention and is not content to have anyone mention him; rather he is made like a jester, neither angered for him nor against him.

The third is nabz, which is lower than the second, because in this level one attaches to him a permanent attribute in him that calls for hatred of him and lowering his station. As for nabz, it is merely the naming, even if the attribute is not in him. This is because a good title or a pleasing name, when given to someone and attached to him, does not mean that its meaning exists in him. For one who is named Sa'd or Sa'id may not be so; likewise one who is titled Imam al-Din or Husam al-Din is not understood from it to be so; it is only a mark and an ornament. Similarly, nabz with "Marwan," and Marwan (the donkey) was not like that; rather that was a mark and an attribution. The word is not intended as a description unless the attribute is meant by it, just as proper names are like that. For when you say to one named Abd Allah: "You are the slave of Allah, so do not worship other than Him," meaning his description, you have not brought his proper name as a reference. So He said: "Do not be arrogant, so that you belittle your brothers and consider them insignificant, to the point that you pay them no attention at all. And if you descend from this blessing toward them, do not defame them, seeking to lower their rank and diminish their station. And if you abandon looking into their faults and describing them with what defames them, then do not call them by what they dislike, nor exaggerate. This is not a fault to be mentioned in it; it is merely a name uttered without intending to express a description."

He mentions in the verse several issues:

The first issue: His saying ﴿let not a people ridicule another people﴾. Qawm (people) is a noun applied to a group of men, and it does not apply to women or to children, because it is a collective of those who stand (qā'im), like sawm being the plural of sa'im (fasting). Those who stand over affairs are men, so according to this, the qawm are men, not women.

Benefit: The lack of attention and belittling generally proceeds mostly from men toward men, because a woman in herself is weak; when men do not pay attention to her, she has no standing. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Women are flesh on a bone, except what you repel from them." As for women, belittling a man is not found among them, and their lack of attention to him is due to their need to meet their needs through him. As for men toward men and women toward women, this kind of ugliness is found among them, and this is more well known.

The second issue: He said at the highest level, which is the extreme of what is reprehensible: ﴿perhaps they may be better than them﴾, as a breaking of him and a hatred of his denial. And at the second level He said: ﴿nor defame one another﴾, making them as themselves, since when they descend one degree, Allah raises them one degree. In the first, He made the one ridiculed the better; in the second, He made the one ridiculed an example. In His saying ﴿perhaps they may be better than them﴾ there is wisdom: that He found in them the denial that leads to neglect, and made himself better than them, as Iblis did when he did not regard Adam and said: ﴿I am better than him﴾ [Sad: 76], so he became the better. It may be said: the intent of His saying "they may be" (an yakunu) is "they may become," for whoever belittles a person for his poverty, loneliness, or weakness is not safe from becoming poor himself while the poor becomes rich, or from becoming weak while the weak becomes strong.

The third issue: Allah the Exalted said: ﴿a people from a people﴾ and did not say: "a soul from a soul." This is because it contains an indication of prohibiting arrogance, and the arrogant in most matters displays his tyranny before the eyes of witnesses; but when he gathers in private with one who is not regarded in the congregation, he makes himself humble. So He addressed them with the word qawm, as a prohibition for them from what they do.

The fourth issue: His saying the Exalted: ﴿and do not defame yourselves﴾. In it are two aspects:

One of them: that the blame of a brother returns to the brother; so when someone blames a person, it is as if he has blamed himself.

The second: that when he blames him, while he himself is not free of a fault, the one blamed fights him and blames him, so he, by his fault, causes the other to fault him, and it is as if he himself is the one who blames himself. On this is interpreted His saying: ﴿and do not kill yourselves﴾ [an-Nisa: 29], meaning that if you kill a soul, you will be killed, so you will be as if you killed yourselves. It may bear a third aspect: that you say: do not blame yourselves, meaning each one of you, for if you do so, you have blamed yourselves, meaning each one blames each one, and you become blamers from one aspect and blamed from another. This aspect is evident here, but not so in His saying: ﴿and do not kill yourselves﴾.

The fifth issue: If it is said: You have mentioned that this is guidance for the believers on what the believer must do when present, after the reference to what he does in absence. But His saying ﴿and do not defame﴾ has been said to mean: the blame behind a person, while al-hamz is the blame to a person's face. We say: it is not so; rather the opposite is more fitting. For when we look at the inversion of the letters, they indicate the opposite: lamaza, when inverted, becomes lazama, and hamaza, when inverted, becomes hazama. The first indicates closeness, and the second indicates distance. If it is said: lamz is the attack and blame to the face, it would be more fitting, even though each is said with one meaning.

The sixth issue: Allah the Exalted said: ﴿nor call one another by offensive nicknames﴾ and did not say: "la tanbizu." This is because when the one who defames defames, the one defamed may not find in him at that moment a fault to blame him with, and so he searches and follows him to find a fault in him; thus defamation arises from one side. But as for nabz, no one is unable to bring it, for whoever calls another by "donkey," the other calls him by "bull" or something else. Evidently, nabz leads immediately to mutual nicknaming, and defamation does not.

As for His saying the Exalted: ﴿how wicked is the name of wickedness after faith﴾.

It has been said: the meaning is: how wicked is it that one says to a Muslim, "O Jew," after faith, meaning after he has believed; so how wicked is it to name him a disbeliever. It may bear a better aspect than this, which is that this completes the admonition, as if He said: "O you who believe, let not a people ridicule another people, nor defame, nor call one another by nicknames; for if one does so, he becomes wicked after having believed, and it is ugly for the believer to commit wickedness after his faith." So His saying: ﴿those who believe and do not mix their faith with wrongdoing﴾ [al-An'am: 82] is "how wicked is wickedness after faith," and how wicked it is that you be called wicked because of these acts after you have been named believers.

He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And whoever does not repent, then those are the wrongdoers﴾. This may bear two meanings:

One of them: these are among the minor sins, so whoever persists in them becomes a wrongdoer and a wicked person, but with a single instance one is not characterized by wrongdoing or wickedness. So He said: whoever does not leave them and makes them a habit, he is a wrongdoer.

The second: His saying the Exalted: ﴿let not a people ridicule﴾, ﴿nor defame﴾, ﴿nor call one another by nicknames﴾ is a prohibition for them against these in the future, and His saying: ﴿and whoever does not repent﴾ commands them to repent of what has passed and to show regret for it, as an exaggeration in warning and a tightening in restraint. The original form of His saying: ﴿nor call one another by nicknames﴾ is "la tatanabazu," and one of the two tas was dropped, as in the interrogative one of the two hamzas was dropped, when He said: ﴿It is the same for them whether you warn them or not﴾ [al-Baqarah: 6]. Deletion is better here, because the taa of address and the taa of the doer are two letters of one kind in one word, whereas the interrogative hamza is a word by itself, and the hamza of "anzarta" is another; and bearing two letters in two words is easier than bearing them in one word. For this reason, idgham (assimilation) is obligatory in our saying "madda," but it is not obligatory in our saying "amdud," nor in our saying "marra" versus "imrur bina."

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿O you who have believed, avoid much of suspicion; indeed, some suspicion is sin. And do not spy, and do not backbite one another. Would one of you like to eat the flesh of his brother when he is dead? You would detest it. And fear God; indeed, God is Accepting of repentance, Merciful.﴾

The reason is that suspicion is the cause of what has preceded it, and upon it vices are built, and from it the hidden enemy appears. The speaker, when he bases his affairs upon certainty, rarely becomes certain of a fault in anyone so that he would blame him for it, for the act may appear to be ugly while in reality it is not so, since its doer may be heedless or the observer may be mistaken. His saying (much) is an exclusion of those suspicions upon which good things are built. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Think well of the believer." In sum, every matter whose foundation is not certainty, suspicion regarding it is not something to be avoided. An example of this is the judgment of the judge on the testimony of witnesses, and the presumption of innocence in the absence of witnesses, and so on. So His saying ﴿avoid much﴾ and His saying, exalted is He, ﴿indeed, some suspicion is sin﴾ is an indication of taking the more cautious course, just as a dangerous road does not always have a highwayman on it, yet you do not travel it merely because this happens on it once or twice, unless it is necessary, in which case you travel it with a company. Likewise, suspicion is appropriate after thorough striving and reaching firm confidence.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And do not spy﴾, completing what preceded; for when He, exalted is He, said: ﴿avoid much of suspicion﴾, it was understood from it that what is considered is certainty. So the speaker says: "I will uncover so-and-so," meaning: I will know him with certainty and inspect his fault by direct observation, and then I will blame him, and thus I will have avoided suspicion. So God, exalted is He, said: do not seek suspicion, and do not strive to attain certainty concerning the faults of people.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And let not some of you backbite others﴾, as an indication of the obligation to protect the honor of the believer in his absence. In this there are several meanings:

First: In His saying, exalted is He, ﴿some of you [backbite] others﴾, it is in reality general, like His saying: ﴿And do not defame yourselves﴾. As for the one who backbites, the backbiter first knows his own fault, so his act is not to be interpreted as backbiting him; hence He did not say: "do not backbite yourselves," because backbiting does not prompt the one backbited to take up the fault of the one who backbites him, whereas a fault prompts a fault.

Second: If someone says: this meaning was already achieved by His saying, exalted is He, "do not backbite," without restricting it? We say: No, because what is forbidden is backbiting a believer, so He said ﴿some of you [backbite] others﴾. As for the disbeliever, he is openly declared and mentioned for what is in him; and how not, when the wicked person may be mentioned for what is in him when there is need.

Third: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Would one of you like to eat the flesh of his brother when he is dead?﴾ is evidence that the backbiting that is forbidden is backbiting of a believer, not mentioning a disbeliever, for He likened it to eating the flesh of a brother, and He had said earlier: ﴿The believers are only brothers﴾. So there is no brotherhood except among believers, and there is no prohibition except concerning something resembling eating the flesh of a brother. Therefore in this verse there is a prohibition against backbiting a believer, not a disbeliever.

Fourth: What is the wisdom in this comparison? We say: it is an indication that a person's honor is like his blood and flesh, and this is of the type of apparent analogy, for a man's honor is more noble than his flesh. So if it is not good for a sensible person to eat the flesh of people, it is not good for him to tear at their honor by a better argument, for that is more painful. His saying ﴿the flesh of his brother﴾ is more emphatic in prohibition, because the enemy is carried by anger to chew the flesh of an enemy; so He said: the truest of friends is the one your mother bore, so eating his flesh is the ugliest of things. His saying, exalted is He, (dead) is an indication of removing a

So He said: eating the flesh of a brother, while he is dead, also causes no pain, yet it is in the extreme of ugliness, because if he became aware of it he would be pained, just as a dead person, if he sensed his flesh being eaten, would be pained by it. Within this there is also a meaning: that backbiting is like eating the flesh of a human being when dead, and it is not lawful to eat it except for the one under compulsion, to the extent of need; and one under compulsion who finds the flesh of a dead sheep and the flesh of a dead human does not eat the flesh of a human; likewise the backbiter, if he finds for his need a means of repelling it other than backbiting, then backbiting is not permitted to him. His saying, exalted is He, (dead) is a circumstantial qualifier of either the flesh or the brother. If it is said: flesh cannot be dead, we say: Indeed, the Prophet ﷺ said: "What is cut off from a living thing is dead," and he called the clot dead. If it is said: when we make it a circumstantial qualifier of the brother, it is neither the doer nor the object, so it is not permissible to make it a circumstantial qualifier, as one says: "I passed by my brother Zayd standing," meaning Zayd was standing. We say: it is permissible to say: whoever eats his flesh has eaten him, so the brother becomes the eaten object; unlike passing by my brother Zayd. It is permissible to say: "I struck his face sinning," meaning: while he is sinning, namely the owner of the face, just as when you strike his face you have struck him. But it is not permissible to say: "I tore his garment sinning," making the sinner a circumstantial qualifier of someone other than you.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿so you detested it﴾ contains two issues:

The first issue: The pronoun referring back to it may have several possibilities. The first, and the most apparent, is that it refers to the eating, for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Would one of you like that he eat﴾ means: would one of you like the eating; since "that" with the verb indicates the verbal noun, meaning: so you detested the eating. The second: that it refers to the flesh, i.e., you detested the flesh. The third: that it refers to the dead in His saying (dead), and its implied sense is: Would one of you like that he eat the flesh of his brother dead, rotten, so you detested it. So it is as if it were a qualifier of His saying (dead), and there is in it extra emphasis in warning: that a carcass, if eaten in rare circumstances due to some rare cause, but when it has become foul, stinking and rotten, is not eaten at all; likewise backbiting should be.

The second issue: The fa' in His saying ﴿so you detested it﴾ requires a connection. What is it? We say: there are several aspects:

One: that it is the implied answer to a statement, as if, when He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Would one of you like﴾, it was said in reply: "that."

Second: that the interrogative in His saying ﴿Would one of you like﴾ is for denial, as if He said: none of you would like to eat the flesh of his brother dead; so you detested it then; and no supposition is needed.

Third: that this connection is the connection of the effect to its cause and its consequence upon it, as you say: so-and-so came walking and so became tired, because walking produces tiredness; so likewise His saying (dead), for death produces such aversion that a person does not wish to spend the night in a house where there is a dead body, so how would he approach it to the point of eating from it; thus there is in it then a severe aversion; likewise it should be the state regarding backbiting.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And fear God; indeed, God is Accepting of repentance, Merciful.﴾ It is a conjunction upon what preceded of commands and prohibitions, i.e., avoid and fear. In the verse there are subtleties: among them, that God, exalted is He, mentioned in this verse three matters in order. Their explanation is that He, exalted is He, said: ﴿avoid much﴾, i.e., do not say concerning the believers what you do not know of them, based on suspicion. Then, if you are asked about things merely suspected, do not say: "we will uncover their affairs so as to become certain of them before mentioning them." Then, if you know something of them without spying, do not say it, do not spread it about them, and do not blame them. So in the first there is a prohibition against what is not known; then a prohibition against seeking that knowledge; then a prohibition against mentioning what has been known. Among them also: God, exalted is He, did not say: "avoid saying a matter contrary to what you know," nor did He say: "avoid doubt"; rather the first thing He forbade is speaking on the basis of suspicion. That is because speaking contrary to knowledge is lying and fabrication, and speaking with doubt and conjecture about the unseen is foolishness and mockery, and both are in the extreme of ugliness; so He did not forbid it explicitly, relying on His saying, exalted is He, (O you who have believed), for their being described as believers prevents them from fabrication and doubt, which is the habit of the disbeliever. He only forbade them from what is frequently found among Muslims; for this reason He said in the verse: ﴿let not a people ridicule [another people]﴾. Among them also: He concluded the two verses with mention of repentance. But in the first verse, since it began with a prohibition in His saying ﴿let not a people ridicule a people﴾, He mentioned negation, which is close to prohibition; and in the second verse, since it began with a command in His saying ﴿avoid﴾, He mentioned doubt, which is close to command.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿O mankind, indeed We created you from male and female and made you peoples and tribes that you may know one another. Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you. Indeed, Allah is Knowing and Acquainted.﴾

It is an explanation and affirmation of what preceded it. This is because mocking others and defaming them, if it is due to a difference in religion and faith, is permissible, since we have explained that His saying ﴿And do not backbite one another﴾ and His saying ﴿And do not defame yourselves﴾ prohibit defaming and backbiting a believer. But if it is not due to that cause, it is not permissible. This is because people in general, whether disbelievers or believers, share in what the boaster boasts of other than faith and disbelief. If the boasting is due to wealth, then a disbeliever may be wealthy and a believer poor, and vice versa. If it is due to lineage, then a disbeliever may be of noble descent and a believer may be a black slave, and vice versa. Thus, in what is not of religion and piety, people are equal and similar. None of these things has any effect in the absence of piety. Every person who adheres to a religion knows that whoever agrees with him in his religion is more noble than whoever opposes him in it, even if the latter is of higher lineage or greater wealth. How then should one who possesses the true religion, and is firmly grounded in it, be surpassed by one who falls short of him in it because of something other than it? His saying, exalted is He, ﴿O mankind, indeed We created you from male and female﴾ has two possible meanings:

First: [it refers to] Adam and Eve.

Second: [it means] each one of you, the people present at the time of the address, We created from a father and a mother.

If we say that the intended meaning is the first, then this is an indication that some should not boast over others, because they are all children of one man and one woman. If we say that the intended meaning is the second, then this is an indication that the species is one, since each one was created as the other was, from a father and a mother. The difference is within the species, not a difference between two species. Indeed, among the laws of difference is that the difference cannot be measured between a fly and a wolf. But the difference among people by way of disbelief and faith is like the difference between two species, because the disbeliever is inanimate in a sense, as he is like livestock, rather even more astray. The believer is a human being in the meaning in which a human being ought to be. Difference among human beings is a difference in sensation, not in species, since all of them are from male and female. Therefore, in this comparison, no consideration remains for that. There are issues concerning this:

The first issue: If it is said that this is based on not considering lineage, and that is not the case, since lineage has consideration both by custom and by Sharia, to the extent that a noblewoman may not be married to a Nabatean [a man of low standing], then we say: when a great matter comes, a lowly matter no longer has consideration. This holds in sensation, in Sharia, and in custom. As for sensation, the stars are not seen at sunrise, and the wing of a fly has a buzz that is not heard when there is loud thunder. As for custom, whoever comes with the king no longer has any consideration, nor does anyone turn toward him. [Page 118 ends here]

Once you know this regarding these two, then it is so in Sharia as well. When the divine religious nobility comes, no consideration remains there for any matter, neither for lineage nor for wealth. Do you not see that the disbeliever, even if he is of the highest lineage, and the believer, even if he is of the lowest lineage, cannot be compared to one another? Likewise, whatever is with something else. For this reason, every noble and every lowly person is suitable for religious offices such as judgeship and testimony, provided he is pious, learned, and righteous, and no sinner is suitable for any of them, even if he is of Quraysh lineage and of Qarun's wealth. But if two people share firm religion, and one of them is of noble descent, he is preferred by lineage in the eyes of people, but not in the eyes of Allah. This is because Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿And that man will have nothing except what he strives for﴾ [al-Najm: 39], and the nobility of lineage is not acquired and is not obtained by striving.

The second issue: What is the wisdom in choosing lineage from among the causes of boasting, and not mentioning wealth? We say: Among the things people boast of in this world, though they are many, lineage is the highest of them. This is because wealth may come to a poor person, and so the boaster's boasting of it is nullified. Beauty, youth, and other things are not lasting and permanent. Lineage is constant and enduring, and it cannot be acquired by one who does not have it. So Allah chose it for mention and nullified its consideration in relation to piety, so that by a stronger argument it would be known that the nullification of other things is even more certain.

The third issue: If the purpose of the verse is to show that it is impermissible to boast by other than piety, is there any benefit in His saying ﴿indeed We created you﴾? We say: Yes. This is because everything that is preferred over another is preferred either by something that attaches to it and comes about after its existence, or by something that precedes it. What comes after it, such as beauty, strength, and other attributes sought in that thing, and what precedes it is either related to the origin from which it came into being, or to the agent who brought it into existence. As it is said of two vessels: this is of copper and this is of silver; and it is said: this is the work of so-and-so and this is the work of so-and-so. So He, exalted is He, said: there is no preference in what you were created from, since you are all from male and female, nor by regard to the makers, since you were all created by Allah. Therefore, if there is a difference among you, it occurs through matters that attach to you and come about after your existence, and the noblest of them is piety and nearness to Allah, exalted is He.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And made you peoples and tribes﴾, and regarding this there are two meanings:

First: ﴿And We made you peoples﴾ dispersed, whose gatherer is not known, like the non-Arabs. And tribes, whose gatherer is a known single [ancestor], like the Arabs and the Children of Israel.

Second: ﴿And We made you peoples﴾ included within tribes. For under the tribe are the peoples, under the peoples are the clans, under the clans are the subclans, under the subclans are the branches, under the branches are the relatives. He mentioned the more general term because it is more conducive to boasting, since in the more general category there enter innumerable rich and poor, and countless weak and strong. Then He explained the benefit of this, which is mutual acquaintance, and in this there are two meanings:

First: The benefit of this is mutual support, not mutual boasting.

Second: Its benefit is acquaintance, not mutual denial. Mockery, defamation, and backbiting lead to mutual denial, not to acquaintance. In this there are subtle meanings. The first: He, exalted is He, said ﴿indeed We created you﴾ and said ﴿We made you﴾, because creation is a root from which making into peoples branches off. For the first is creation and bringing into existence, then the attribution of what they are attributed with. But making into peoples is for mutual acquaintance, and creation is for worship, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And I did not create jinn and humankind except to worship Me﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 56]. The consideration of the root precedes the consideration of the branch. So know that lineage is considered after the consideration of worship, just as the making into peoples comes to be after the creation comes to be. So if there is worship among you, your lineages are considered among you; otherwise, they are not. The second: His saying ﴿created you﴾ and ﴿made you﴾ is an indication of the impermissibility of boasting, because that is not due to your striving, and you have no power over any of it. How then do you boast of what has no part for you in it? If it is said: guidance and misguidance are likewise, due to His saying ﴿Indeed We guided him to the way﴾ [al-Insan: 3] and ﴿by which He guides whom He wills﴾ [al-Shura: 52], we say: Allah has established for us an acquisition in it [Page 119 begins here] based on action, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿So whoever wills takes to his Lord a way﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 19].

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And you do not will except that Allah wills﴾ [al-Insan: 30]. But as for lineage, there is no such acquisition. The third: His saying ﴿that you may know one another﴾ is an indication of a hidden analogy, and its explanation is that He, exalted is He, said: indeed you were made tribes so that you may know one another. If you are closer to a noble person in whom you take pride, then He created you so that you may know your Lord. So if you are closer to Him, and He is the most noble of existent beings, then the most deserving of boasting there, above all, is boasting in that. The fourth: In it is guidance to a proof that shows boasting is not by lineages. This is because tribes are for mutual acquaintance through affiliation to a person. If that person is noble, then boasting is valid in your estimation, and if he is not noble, it is not valid. The nobility of that man whom you boast of is either by affiliation to a clan, or by acquiring a virtue. If it is by affiliation, then it must end at a point. If it is by acquisition, then the religious, learned, generous, and benevolent person becomes like the one whom the boaster boasts of. So how does one boast of a father and a grandfather over someone who has obtained through good fortune and goodness what has made himself superior to that father and grandfather?! Unless one attains the nobility of affiliation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), for no one comes near the Messenger in virtue to the point of saying "I am like your father." But in this lineage, the Prophet (ﷺ) established nobility for whoever is affiliated to him by acquisition, and negated it for whoever wanted nobility by mere affiliation. He said: "We, the company of prophets, are not inherited from," and he said: "The scholars are the heirs of the prophets," meaning: we are not inherited from by affiliation; rather we are inherited from by acquisition.

I heard that one of the nobles in the lands of Khurasan was the closest of people in lineage to Ali (peace be upon him), except that he was a sinner. There was a black client there who had advanced in knowledge and action, and people were inclined to seek blessing from him. It happened that one day he came out of his house heading to the mosque, and a crowd followed him. The noble met him while drunk, and people used to drive the noble away and keep him off the road. He overpowered them and clung to the edges of the shaykh's garment, and said to him: "O black one of the hooves and the eyelashes! O disbeliever, son of a disbeliever! I am the son of the Messenger of Allah! I am humiliated and you are honored! I am reviled and you are praised! I am insulted and you are helped!" The people intended to strike him, but the shaykh said: "No, this is tolerable from him because of his grandfather, and striking him is a punishment for his offense. But O noble one, you have whitened my inner self and blackened your own inner self. So people see the whiteness of my heart above the blackness of my face, and I am honored, and you took the conduct of your father and I took the conduct of my father. So the people saw me in the conduct of your father and saw you in the conduct of my father, and they thought me the son of your father and thought you the son of my father, so they treated you as one treats my father, and treated me as one treats your father!"

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you﴾. Regarding this there are two meanings:

First: The meaning is that whoever is more righteous will be more noble in the sight of Allah, that is, piety produces nobility.

Second: The meaning is that whoever is more noble in the sight of Allah will be more righteous, that is, nobility produces piety, as one says: "The sincere ones are in great danger." The first is more well known, and the second is more apparent, because the term mentioned second should be understood as referring to the term mentioned first in the apparent sense, so one would say: nobility is for piety. But the most general of the two in what is well known is the first. One says: "The most delicious of foods is the sweetest," meaning that the delight is in proportion to the sweetness, not that the sweetness is in proportion to the delight. This statement establishes that piety precedes every virtue. If it is said: piety is among the deeds, and knowledge is more noble, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "One jurist is more severe against the devil than a thousand worshippers," we say: piety is the fruit of knowledge. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Only those among His servants who have knowledge fear Allah﴾ [Fatir: 28]. So there is no piety except for the one who has knowledge. The pious knowing person has perfected his knowledge, and the one who has knowledge but is not pious is like a tree with no fruit. But a fruitful tree is more noble than a tree that does not bear fruit, which is merely firewood. Likewise, the one who has knowledge but is not pious is fuel for Hell. As for the worshipper whom Allah prefers over the jurist, he is the one who has no knowledge, and in that case he does not possess a complete measure of the fear of Allah. Perhaps he worships out of fear of being thrown into the Fire, so he is like one who is compelled, or for entry into Paradise, so he acts like one who works for a wage and returns to his house. The pious one is the one who knows Allah, who is constant at His door, that is, who is near to His presence, and who spends the night with Him. There are issues concerning this:

First topic: the address is to people in general. Honour (al-akram) implies that all share in dignity, and the disbeliever has no honour, for he is more astray than cattle and more abject than vermin. We say: that does not follow, although it is established by the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And We have certainly honoured the children of Adam﴾ [al-Isra: 70], because everyone who is created has acknowledged his Lord. It is as if Allah the Exalted said: whoever persists in it, if he increases, his honour is increased; and whoever turns away from it, the effect of honour is removed from him.

The second: what is the limit of taqwa (God-consciousness), and who is the most God-conscious? We say: the lowest level of taqwa is that the servant avoids what is forbidden and performs what is commanded, and he is not at rest and does not feel secure except with these. If it happens that he commits a forbidden act, he does not feel secure or rely on it, but follows it with a good deed and shows regret and repentance over it. Whenever he commits a forbidden act and does not repent immediately, and relies on respite in the term of life, and the prolongation of hope prevents him from remembrance, then he is not God-conscious. As for the most God-conscious (al-atqa), he is the one who does what he is commanded and leaves what he is forbidden, and he, along with that, fears his Lord and does not occupy himself with other than Allah, so Allah illuminates his heart. If he turns for a moment to his self or his child, he counts that as his sin. For the first group there is salvation, by the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Then We shall save those who were God-conscious﴾ [Maryam: 72]. For the others there is being driven toward Paradise, by the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, the most honourable of you in the sight of Allah is the most God-conscious of you﴾. The difference between one whom the ruler has given a garden and settled in it, and one whom he has chosen for himself and who gains gardens and estates every day through nearness to him, is a great difference.
